H5267.portee: This passage reminds the reader that faithfulness to God may require enduring violence and rejection from the powerful. Although Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are thrown into the fire, the rest of the story reveals that God protects them — a promise of comfort for any believer who is persecuted.

sens: Deity worshiped in Nineveh
Idol represented by a human figure with an eagle's head
H5268.detail: 1. Nisroc is a deity worshiped by the Assyrians in Nineveh, the capital of their empire. King Sennacherib prayed to him in his temple (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38). 2. This idol took the form of a hybrid creature: a human body topped with an eagle's head, a majestic and powerful image intended to embody divine greatness in Assyrian religion.
H5268.origine: The name literally means "the great eagle" in ancient Assyrian. The eagle, a majestic and dominant bird, symbolized divine and royal power in the religions of the ancient Near East. Nisroc thus represents one of the many foreign deities worshiped in the empires of the Fertile Crescent, far from the knowledge of the true God of Israel.
H5268.emploi: Nisroc appears only twice in the Bible, in two parallel accounts: 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38. Both passages recount the same event: the death of King Sennacherib, murdered by his sons while he was praying in the temple of Nisroc. This Assyrian idol is never worshiped in Israel nor praised; it appears only as the god of a foreign and hostile power, underscoring that the worship of false gods belongs to nations that ignore the Lord.
H5268.portee: The existence of Nisroc reminds us that many peoples worshiped deities shaped by human hands, without knowing the living God. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to see that any worship that does not recognize the God of Israel, revealed in Jesus Christ, can only lead to error and ruin — here, Sennacherib meets his death in the temple of his false god.

sens: Boundary location of the territory of Zebulun
H5269.detail: 1. Néa is a locality that marks the boundary of the territory assigned to the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the Promised Land. The Hebrew name evokes a sensation of shaking or agitation, but here it designates a fixed geographical point serving as a landmark for tribal borders (Joshua 19:13).
H5269.origine: The Hebrew name נֵעָה (néa) comes from a root that means "to shake" or "to tremble," but its application to this place remains obscure. The biblical text mentions it as a variant or another name for Néiel (נְעִיאֵל), an important town in the northern coastal region of the Land of Israel.
H5269.emploi: Néa appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:13, in the list of borders and cities of the territory of Zebulun. It is cited there as a geographical landmark used to delineate the possessions of this tribe during the land distribution after the conquest.

sens: One of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh
H5270.detail: Noa is one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a man of the tribe of Manasseh during the Exodus. Her sisters were Mahlah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. These five daughters became famous in Israel's history because their father had no sons: they presented themselves before Moses to request their inheritance, which led God to establish a new law regarding succession (Numbers 27:1-11). Noa is mentioned each time the Bible lists these five daughters, particularly in the account of their marriage to their uncles' sons (Numbers 36:11), where she remains faithful to the tribe of Manasseh by marrying a man from her own family.
H5270.origine: The name Noa means "movement" in Hebrew. There is no other character bearing this name in the Bible, making this woman a unique and memorable figure in the biblical narrative.
H5270.emploi: Noa is mentioned four times in the Bible, always as one of the five daughters of Zelophehad. She first appears in the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 26:33), then during the request for inheritance presented by these daughters to Moses (Numbers 27:1), next when the Bible reports their marriage (Numbers 36:11), and finally in the allocation of the territory of Canaan according to the tribes (Joshua 17:3). Her story illustrates how courageous women obtained legal rights in a society where women normally did not inherit.
H5270.portee: The story of Noa and her sisters shows that God listens to those who present their requests with justice and confidence. These women changed the law of Israel by daring to ask for equality before God, reminding the Christian reader that the voices of the small and marginalized matter in the eyes of the Lord.

sens: the period of life from childhood to adulthood
the time of beginnings, origins
the acts or responsibilities of someone in their youth
the inexperience or innocence of young age
the vigor and freshness characteristic of this age
H5271A.detail: 1. Youth is primarily the season of life before maturity, when one is young. It characterizes a period where everything begins: thoughts, experiences, mistakes. In Genesis 8:21, God speaks of "the thoughts of man's heart" which are "evil from his youth," showing that the tendencies toward sin date back to childhood. 2. The word also designates the time of beginnings, the original epoch. In Isaiah 47:15, the text speaks of those "with whom you have trafficked from your youth," evoking long-established relationships. 3. Youth can encompass all the acts and responsibilities of a person at this age. In Jeremiah 31:19, the man confesses: "I bear the shame of my youth," carrying the shame of what he did or committed when he was young. 4. It also evokes innocence or inexperience: in Ezekiel 16:22, it speaks of "your virgin breast," showing the purity of one who has not yet tasted experiences. 5. Finally, it expresses strength and vigor: in Psalms 103:5, the text says that God "renews your youth like the eagle," renewing the strength of youth.
H5271A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of awakening, rising, coming out of sleep — the image of the young who "rises" or "awakens" to life. This root is also found in other words of the same family. The word thus evokes the idea of a new beginning, of a nascent strength. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word was rendered by terms like "neos" (new, young) which also express this idea of beginning and renewal.
H5271A.emploi: The word appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic (Psalms, Proverbs), prophetic (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), and historical books. It almost always designates the period of young age, but with nuances depending on the context. Among the psalmists, it is the time when one remembers God (Psalms 25:7, "remember... my youth"). Among the prophets, it often becomes a time of guilt: Israel remembers the day of its youth when it loved the Lord (Jeremiah 2:2), but also all the sins committed at that age (Ezekiel 23:3 and following). The word can also designate a moment of innocence that has been abused: in Proverbs 2:17 and Malachi 2:15, it refers to a young wife. In Psalms 127:4, youth is the most desirable time of life: "children born in one's youth" are a blessing for a man.
H5271A.portee: This word reminds us that youth is not an unimportant time, but a period where convictions and habits are formed that mark a whole life. It can be the seat of innocence and communion with God, but also that of sin and error: that is why so many biblical passages urge the young to flee from evil. For today's believer, it is a call to take seriously the choices and attachments of their youth, as they shape the rest of their life.

sens: The period of life from childhood to adulthood
The state or condition of one who is young
The initial, formative period of a person or a nation
H5271B.detail:
1. Youth is primarily the period of life when one grows, between childhood and adulthood. It is the time of formation, where habits and dispositions are forged. In Jeremiah 32:30, the Lord reminds the children of Israel that "from their youth" they have committed evil before Him: the word evokes the initial and decisive moment when choices are made.
2. The word also designates the state of youth itself, that is, this period characterized by strength, energy, and inexperience. It is at this time that generations define themselves in relation to God.
3. In a broader sense, "youth" can designate the time of beginning or formation — not only of a person but also of a people. Israel showed its unfaithfulness not late, but "from its youth," as if it were a constitutive flaw.
H5271B.origine: The word הברי (néourim) comes from a root that evokes the energy and vigor characteristic of young age. It is a variant or a related form to נְעוּרִים (H5271A), with the same root. In Hebrew, words of this family express the idea of raw strength and lack of wisdom — which characterizes the young who do not yet have the experience of the old.
H5271B.emploi: This word is rare in the Bible; it appears only once in the Segond translations, in Jeremiah 32:30. However, it belongs to a family of terms that the Bible frequently uses to speak of the youth of the people of Israel or individuals. The context shows that youth is not merely a chronological backdrop: it is the period that God invites the people to examine, for it is then that spiritual orientations are set. Jeremiah reminds us that evil is not a late deviation of Israel, but a habit contracted from the very beginning of its existence.
H5271B.portee: This word challenges the believer regarding the importance of the choices and orientations of their youth. Indeed, according to the Bible, youth is not just a transitional phase, but a time when spiritual directions are engraved in the soul that will mark the whole life. Jeremiah shows that a nation — and by extension, a person — bears the fruits of its early choices. It is an implicit exhortation to train the young in the fear of God, for what is learned and chosen in youth lasts long.

sens: City on the border of the territory of Asher in the Promised Land
H5272.detail: Neiel is a city located on the border of the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of the Promised Land. It is mentioned in the description of the boundaries of this territory, between Beth-Dagon and Cabul (Joshua 19:27). Its precise location remains uncertain, but it marked an important geographical landmark for delineating the lands of Asher.
H5272.origine: The name Neiel literally means "moved by God" or "movement of God," composed of Hebrew that evokes the action of moving or being set in motion. Although it is a proper name of a place, it carries a theological dimension reminding us that it is God who directs the movement and establishment of the boundaries of His people.
H5272.emploi: Neiel appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:27, in the passage where Moses enumerates the cities and boundaries of the territory of Asher after the conquest of Canaan. It is among a long list of geographical landmarks used to precisely delineate the lands assigned to each tribe. Its uniqueness in the biblical text suggests that it was a small settlement or an important natural landmark for the inhabitants of the time, but it did not play a significant historical or religious role in the biblical narrative.

sens: That which pleases the senses, that which is sweet and delightful to taste, hear, or feel
That which is beautiful, attractive, appealing to the eye
That which brings joy, happiness, satisfaction
That which is favorable, sympathetic, benevolent towards someone
H5273A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates that which directly pleases the body or the senses: something sweet, delightful. It is the pleasant sensation one experiences in the presence of something good. Thus, in Psalms 16:11, the "eternal pleasures" are the complete joys that await the faithful beside God.
2. It also describes physical beauty: that which is beautiful to see, attractive. In Song of Solomon 1:16, the beloved is beautiful, "pleasant" to behold.
3. The word expresses inner joy, the happiness brought by a situation. In Psalms 133:1, it is "good," meaning happy and beneficial, for brothers to dwell together — harmony is a good that rejoices the heart.
4. It also qualifies a benevolent, favorable attitude: God is "favorable" (Psalms 135:3), meaning He welcomes us with kindness and treats us with goodness.
H5273A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes sweetness and pleasure. It belongs to the family of words describing that which delights and satisfies. The basic image is that of what charms the senses and the heart. In Hebrew, this root opposes bitterness and displeasure: it speaks of all that is desirable and good.
H5273A.emploi: This word appears about eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic (Psalms, Proverbs, Song of Solomon) and historical books. It describes both physical and material realities (a beautiful and favorable inheritance in Psalms 16:6, a dwelling filled with pleasant things in Proverbs 24:4) as well as inner states (joy, happiness). Its meaning also encompasses moral and spiritual appreciation: that which is pleasing to God, what delights Him, and what pleases pious men. The usages show that the pleasure it describes is never superficial: it is that of the heart that finds deep satisfaction, of heaven that recognizes divine beauty.
H5273A.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is not an enemy of joy, beauty, and goodness. Life with God is not endless austerity, but it leads to "eternal pleasures" (Psalms 16:11). It also invites us to recognize the beautiful and pleasant in fraternal harmony and in God's gifts, without idolizing them — it is a call to gratitude and praise for the blessings received.

sens: That which pleases the ear, that which sounds good, that which is harmonious
That which is sweet, suave, delightful to taste or touch
That which is pleasing, beautiful, attractive
H5273B.detail: 1. The primary sense is musical or sonic: a voice, a melody, an instrument that pleases by its acoustic quality. David is called "the pleasant singer of Israel" (2 Samuel 23:1), which means that his way of singing touched the heart; the "melodious" harp of Psalm 81:3 is one that produces harmonious and beautiful sounds. 2. By extension, the word designates that which is sweet and flavorful to taste or touch, that which brings pleasure. 3. In a figurative sense, it expresses all that is beautiful, attractive, pleasing to see or experience.
H5273B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be sweet, to be pleasant." It is related to other words in the same family that express sweetness, suavity, and pleasantness. In biblical Hebrew, this root is linked to the fundamental idea of pleasure and beauty that delights the senses.
H5273B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first qualifies David himself as "the pleasant singer of Israel," emphasizing that his voice and music had an exceptional quality that deeply touched. It also describes the "melodious harp" in a psalm inviting to praise, where the instrument must produce beautiful and harmonious music to celebrate God. Both usages concern music and praise, areas where sensory pleasure serves to honor God.
H5273B.portee: This word reminds us that God appreciates beauty and harmony in praise. David was not only a powerful king but a musician whose voice touched hearts — the Bible thus values artistic talents in the service of God. This encourages us to offer God not only our words but our best, with beauty and heart.

sens: To close a door, to lock it or barricade it with a lock or latch
To be closed, inaccessible, reserved for someone
H5274A.detail:
1. To close a door by locking or barricading it, to prevent it from being opened. It is the concrete action of secure closure. Ehud, after killing King Eglon, "closed the doors of the upper chamber behind him and locked them" (Judges 3:23): he locks the door behind him to buy time before the crime is discovered.
2. To be closed, shut, inaccessible — in a figurative sense, that which is reserved, protected, or belongs exclusively to someone. The beloved in the Song is described as "a closed garden, a sealed fountain" (Song of Solomon 4:12): an image of a chaste and faithful woman, whose access is exclusive.
H5274A.origine: The verb comes from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of closure and securing. It conjugates simply: in its basic form, it means "to close" or "to lock." The word "lock" (also used in the Segond) is a derivative of the same verb, designating the object that closes and locks a door. It is a verb of direct action and common in ancient daily life.
H5274A.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible translated by the Segond. It is used mainly in the context of doors and access to places: in the story of Ehud (Judges 3:23-24), it describes the urgent locking of a door to conceal a crime. In the context of 2 Samuel 13:17-18, it expresses the order to escort and close the door after a woman leaves a room. In Song of Solomon 4:12, the same word takes on a figurative meaning: a beloved "closed" symbolizes a chaste and faithful woman, whose intimacy is sealed. The verb always retains the idea of closure and restriction of access.
H5274A.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on protection, fidelity, and secrecy. In historical narratives, it shows how men seek to secure places and control access. In the Song, it elevates closure to the rank of a symbol: to be closed is not to be cold, but to be precious, reserved, faithful to a unique love. It is a call to protect what is sacred and precious in the life of the heart.

sens: To provide someone with sandals or shoes
To give shoes to someone as a sign of care or protection
H5274B.detail: 1. The verb literally means to put shoes on someone's feet. In 2 Chronicles 28:15, the leaders of Israel "put shoes on" the captives they release, just as they clothe and feed them: it is an act of compassion and restoration. 2. In Ezekiel 16:10, the Lord "puts shoes on" Jerusalem in a vision of marital love: He gives her sandals made of dyed skins, among other signs of dignity and wealth. The verb here expresses how God cares for His people by adorning them with everything suitable for a loving husband.
H5274B.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that designates the sandal or shoe itself. This word belongs to the family of terms related to clothing and bodily equipment. Its concrete usage — putting a shoe on the feet — reflects one of the elementary forms of care one can give to someone.
H5274B.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Old Testament. In 2 Chronicles 28:15, it describes an act of concrete mercy: the Israelites of the Northern Kingdom restore to the captives of the Southern Kingdom not only their belongings but also the clothing and shoes they lack. In Ezekiel 16:10, the same verb is part of an allegory of marriage: God adorns Jerusalem, His chosen bride, with magnificent sandals among many adornments. In both cases, putting shoes on someone is to recognize their dignity and show affection.
H5274B.portee: This verb reminds us that taking care of someone also involves attending to concrete details: their clothing, their feet, their comfort. Acts of mercy are not only spiritual; they touch the whole body. For the Christian, it is a lesson on true compassion, which restores the suffering person in their entirety.

sens: Footwear worn on the feet
An object of value or personal possession
A sign of humility or respect before the sacred
A symbol of a transaction or commitment
A mark of contempt or domination
H5275.detail:
1. The shoe is simply the footwear one wears to walk and protect the feet. It is an ordinary garment, made of leather or durable material. In Isaiah 5:27, the text mentions "the strap of his shoes" which could break during a difficult walk, showing that the shoe is a common and fragile object.
2. The shoe can denote a personal possession, something one owns. In Genesis 14:23, Abram refuses to take "not even a thread, nor a strap of a shoe" to show that he does not want to accept anything in return; the shoe here represents even the smallest of riches.
3. Removing one's shoes expresses humility and respect before a holy place or the presence of God. In Joshua 5:15, the commander of the Lord's army commands Joshua: "Remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy." It is to recognize that one stands before something sacred, greater than oneself.
4. Removing or giving one's shoe seals an agreement or transaction. In Ruth 4:7, the text explains that in the past "to validate any matter relating to a redemption or exchange, one would remove their shoe and give it to the other: this served as a testimony in Israel." The shoe thus becomes a ritual gesture that commits one's word.
5. Throwing one's shoe at someone or a place expresses contempt, domination, or taking possession. In Psalms 60:10, the psalmist cries: "I throw my shoe over Edom," an image of conquest and submission of the enemy.
H5275.origine: The Hebrew word נַעַל (na'al) comes from a root meaning "to bind" or "to attach": the shoe is what is attached to the foot. This etymology explains why shoes were often closed or fastened with straps (as shown by references to the "strap" of the shoe). In Hebrew, the same word also denotes the action of closing or locking; the shoe closes and protects the foot. The family of this word also includes meanings of closure and sealing.
H5275.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in legal, worship, and symbolic contexts. In Exodus 3:5 and Joshua 5:15, removing one's shoes signals a consecrated place where God manifests Himself. In Deuteronomy 25:9 and Ruth 4:7-8, removing or giving one's shoe is a legal act that authenticates a transaction or legal obligation — it was Israel's gesture to conclude an agreement. In Psalms 60:10 and Isaiah 11:15, throwing one's shoe at someone expresses conquest or domination. The context thus varies from the everyday (walking with shoes) to the ritual and symbolic (removing shoes to respect the sacred).
H5275.portee: The shoe in the Bible teaches that even everyday objects can express deep spiritual realities. Removing one's shoes reminds us that we must present ourselves before God with humility and reverence, recognizing that we are merely creatures. The gesture of the shoe in transactions shows how ancient Scripture linked word and visible action: a promise is only true if it is rooted in a concrete action and a visible commitment.

sens: What pleases the senses or the spirit
What brings satisfaction or well-being
What is beautiful or attractive
What causes joy or pleasure
H5276.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes what pleases: a region can be pleasant to live in (Genesis 49:15 describes a resting place where Issachar "sees that the place is pleasant"), a friendship can be pleasant to experience (Jonathan brought David all his "delight"). 2. It also expresses the satisfaction one derives from something: wisdom brings "delight" to the soul, meaning it fills the heart with deep joy (Proverbs 2:10). 3. Sometimes it emphasizes beauty or excellence: wise words are "pleasant" to hear, they attract (Psalms 141:6), just as Song of Solomon 7:7 praises the "pleasant" stature of the beloved. 4. The word can also convey a judgment: he who punishes the wicked finds himself "well off," meaning he feels satisfaction (Proverbs 24:25).
H5276.origine: The Hebrew verb נָעֵם (na'em) expresses the fundamental idea of what pleases or charms. The root evokes a positive sensation, an attraction. The word is found in the expression "Pleasant Days" or in names like Naomi ("my sweetness"), showing that the sense of sweetness and charm is ancient in the Hebrew language.
H5276.emploi: The verb appears about 8 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in the books of poetry and wisdom (Psalms, Proverbs, Song of Solomon). It describes very varied realities: a territory, a friendship, wisdom, physical beauty. Sometimes it carries an ethical nuance: he who punishes the wicked finds himself morally well off. The meaning remains constant — what pleases — but the object changes, showing that pleasure can be physical, emotional, aesthetic, or moral.
H5276.portee: This verb reminds us that God created the world to be beautiful and pleasing to the eyes and heart of man. It also invites the reader to discern what is truly pleasant: a true friendship, wisdom, justice — beyond deceptive pleasures. For the psalmist or the wise, what is pleasant is also what is good, linking beauty to justice.

sens: son of Caleb and grandson of Jephunneh
H5277.detail: Naam is a man of the tribe of Judah, living before the Israelite monarchy. He is the son of Caleb (the famous spy who explored Canaan with Joshua) and the grandson of Jephunneh. According to 1 Chronicles 4:15, his brothers are Iru and Ela.
H5277.origine: The name Naam means "pleasantness" or "sweetness" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing pleasant sweetness. He belongs to the prestigious lineage of Caleb, one of the twelve spies sent by Moses and one of the few from his generation to enter the Promised Land.
H5277.emploi: Naam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:15. This genealogical passage lists the descendants of Caleb and his wife Azubah, notably his sons Iru, Ela, and Naam. This mention, although brief, situates Naam in the honorable lineage of Caleb and testifies to the importance given to the transmission of generations in the genealogy of Judah before the establishment of the monarchy.

sens: Quality of what pleases, what is beautiful and attractive
Sweetness and charm of words or thoughts
Kindness, favor granted
Majestic beauty or splendor
H5278.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what pleases the eye or the heart, what has a natural and attractive beauty. When the psalmist asks to behold the magnificence of the Lord (Psalms 27:4), he speaks of this divine splendor that captivates and delights the gaze.

2. It also applies to the sweetness and charm of words or thoughts. Pleasant words are compared to honey, sweet to the soul and beneficial for the body (Proverbs 16:24), while pleasant thoughts are pure in the eyes of God (Proverbs 15:26).

3. The word also expresses the idea of kindness and favor: the grace of the Lord is a blessing He bestows upon us (Psalms 90:17), a gift of His goodness.

4. It can evoke majestic beauty or impressive splendor, like the pleasant ways of wisdom that lead to peace (Proverbs 3:17).
H5278.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of pleasing and charming. It is related to the notion of what attracts, what enchants. In Zechariah 11:7, the two staffs named "Grace" and "Union" symbolize God's benevolent relationship with His people. This word belongs to the semantic family of goodness and divine favor.
H5278.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs) and the Psalms, plus one occurrence in Zechariah. In Proverbs, it qualifies sweet words and pure thoughts, emphasizing pleasantness and usefulness. In Psalms, it denotes either the majestic beauty of God (Psalms 27:4) or His kindness towards His creatures (Psalms 90:17). In Zechariah, it becomes a symbolic name, showing how God's grace guides and protects His people like a shepherd guides his sheep.
H5278.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's grace is not austere or threatening, but beautiful, attractive, and benevolent. It manifests in the sweetness of wise words and in the splendor of His presence. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek this divine beauty and to let God's grace strengthen His work, recognizing that what is pleasing to God also leads to peace and life.

sens: woman from Ammon
wife of King Solomon
mother of King Rehoboam of Judah
H5279A.detail: Naama is an Ammonite woman who married King Solomon during the reign of the united monarchy of Israel. She is presented in the accounts of 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles as the mother of Rehoboam, who became king of Judah after his father. Her Ammonite origin is emphasized three times in the biblical texts (1 Kings 14:21, 14:31, and 2 Chronicles 12:13), which recalls the marital alliances that Solomon made with neighboring peoples.
H5279A.origine: The name Naama means "charm" or "sweetness" in Hebrew, evoking beauty or pleasantness. The source definition also mentions another Naama, daughter of Lamech before the Flood, but the three biblical usages provided concern only Naama the Ammonite, wife of Solomon.
H5279A.emploi: Naama the Ammonite appears three times in the Bible, always identified as the mother of Rehoboam and the wife of Solomon. 1 Kings 14:21 presents her at the time when Rehoboam becomes king of Judah at forty-one years old. 1 Kings 14:31 mentions her again at the death of Rehoboam. 2 Chronicles 12:13 repeats the information similarly. These three passages systematically emphasize her Ammonite identity, situating Rehoboam in the political context of Solomon's international alliances.
H5279A.portee: Naama reminds us that Solomon allied himself with surrounding nations through marriage, as reported in 1 Kings 11. Her status as queen mother and her royal lineage show how God allowed foreign women to influence the history of His chosen people, but also how these unions sometimes led to spiritual complications for the monarchy of Israel.

sens: City in Lower Judah at the border of Philistine territory
H5279B.detail: Naama is a small town listed among the localities in the region of Lower Judah, on the edge of Philistine territory. It appears in the list of towns in the Judean district, between Beth-Dagon and Makkedah (Joshua 15:41). It was a peripheral locality, marking the transition between the heart of Judah and the coastal lands.
H5279B.origine: The name Naama means "loveliness" (sweetness, grace, charm). It is a common place name in Judah, also borne by other locations. Like many Palestinian names, it reflects a desirable quality of the site or an ancient cult.
H5279B.emploi: Naama appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:41, among the enumeration of cities conquered by the tribe of Judah after entering the Promised Land. This geographical list documents the division of territory. The absence of other mentions suggests it was a small center, without major political or religious role in the history of Israel.

sens: Antediluvian woman, daughter of Lamech and Zillah
Sister of Tubal-Cain, the blacksmith
H5279G.detail:
1. Naama is a woman who lived before the Flood, daughter of Lamech and Zillah. She is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:22, as the sister of Tubal-Cain, the blacksmith who invented bronze and iron tools. She thus symbolizes an antediluvian human lineage endowed with talents and technical know-how.
2. Her sibling relationship with Tubal-Cain situates her in the lineage of Cain and connects her to a time when humanity was already developing arts and crafts before God sent the Flood to judge the world.
H5279G.origine: The name Naama means "grace" or "charm" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes sweetness and pleasantness. This name likely reflects a personal characteristic or a parental wish. In Cain's genealogy, where names carry significant meanings (Tubal-Cain = master of metal, Jubal = he brings), Naama stands out with a name that speaks of beauty rather than technical skill, although she is integrated into a family known for its inventions and advancements.
H5279G.emploi: Naama appears only once in Genesis 4:22. She is presented solely as the sister of Tubal-Cain, without any actions or words of her own. Her role is genealogical: she reminds us that Cain's lineage also included women, and she figures in the tree of human generations before the Flood. The Bible mentions her briefly to complete the picture of Lamech and Zillah's children, in the context where humanity was multiplying and developing technically.

sens: Descendants of Naaman, a man from the tribe of Benjamin
H5280.detail: The Naamanites are the members of the family clan descended from Naaman, son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin. During the census of Israel in the wilderness, Moses records the families descended from each of Benjamin's sons, and thus the descendants of Naaman receive the collective name of "Naamanites" (Numbers 26:40).
H5280.origine: The name comes from Naaman (נַעֲמָן), whose root means "pleasant" or "delightful". The suffix of the demonym adds the meaning of descent: the Naamanites are simply "those who descend from Naaman."
H5280.emploi: The Naamanites are mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the second census of the Israelites, after the first generation in the wilderness. They constitute one of the twelve families descended from Benjamin, alongside the Ardites and nine other clans from the same tribe. This census served to organize the people of Israel before entering Canaan and to allocate the land according to families.

sens: Woman from Bethlehem, wife of Elimelech and mother of Mahlon and Kilion
Mother-in-law of Ruth and Orpah
A woman who knows grief and seeks a future for her daughters-in-law
H5281.detail:
1. Naomi is an Israelite woman from Bethlehem. She marries Elimelech and gives birth to two sons, Mahlon and Kilion. When famine strikes the land, the family exiles to Moab to survive (Ruth 1:2). She embodies the faithful woman of Israel in a foreign land.

2. Naomi becomes a mother-in-law when her two sons marry Moabite women: Ruth and Orpah. After the death of her husband and her sons, she remains alone with her two daughters-in-law (Ruth 1:3-5), in a situation of great precariousness.

3. Naomi goes through the trial of grief and poverty. Upon returning to Bethlehem, she symbolically changes her name, asking to be called Mara (“bitter”) because the Lord has afflicted her (Ruth 1:20-21). She represents the woman who suffers but remains attached to God and cares about the fate of her loved ones.
H5281.origine: The name Naomi means "my joy" or "my sweetness" in Hebrew — a designation full of tenderness that reflects the love and hope of parents. The biblical story presents a striking contrast: at the moment of her impoverished return to Israel, Naomi herself rejects this joyful name to take on the name Mara (“bitter”), acknowledging that her circumstances have transformed her existence. This contrast between the original name and the name of affliction shows how life can strip us of our illusions, and how God remains faithful despite our changes.
H5281.emploi: Naomi appears in the book of Ruth, present in the 21 occurrences of this name. She is a maternal and pious figure who kindly guides Ruth (Ruth 2:22, 3:1) — she knows the laws of Israel and the customs of land redemption. She also represents faith in divine providence: although impoverished, she seeks for her daughters-in-law a rest and marital security (Ruth 3:1), and she recognizes in Boaz a redeemer sent by God (Ruth 2:20). Her story ends in joy when Ruth gives her a grandson, Obed, and the women of Bethlehem exclaim that the Lord has not left her without a protector (Ruth 4:14-17). Naomi moves from grief to hope, from the name of bitterness to the role of a happy grandmother raising a descendant of David.
H5281.portee: Naomi teaches every believer who goes through grief and trial that one must never lose sight of God's faithfulness. Her acceptance of suffering without lasting bitterness, and her ability to rejoice in God's grace towards Ruth and Boaz, show that God restores those who remain faithful to Him. She also embodies maternal love that cares for the well-being of others before oneself, a lesson in selflessness and trust in divine redemption.

sens: Field planted with chosen plants for their beauty or aroma
Garden of delights, expression of human wealth and pride
H5282.detail:
1. The word refers to a field or garden carefully cultivated, where plants — flowers, shrubs, fruit trees — are planted for their visual charm or fragrance, rather than out of necessity. It is a luxury, an ornament. In Isaiah 17:10, the prophet reproaches Judah for having planted these "ornamental plantings" instead of turning to the God who saves them: it is a symbol of the earthly riches in which the people place their trust.
2. The word also evokes pride and carnal confidence in what one possesses. These refined plantings represent material prosperity and worldly pleasures, which divert the heart from God. The prophet denounces this seduction: cultivating ornamentation rather than justice is a spiritual infidelity.
H5282.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be pleasant, sweet, delightful." It is formed on a base evoking pleasure, sweetness, and ornamentation. In the Old Testament, this family of words designates what is beautiful, sweet, or delightful to the senses. The word appears here as the plural feminine form, referring to "plantings" in the sense of ornamental gardens.
H5282.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Isaiah 17:10. The prophet Isaiah uses it to show how Israel has forgotten God by focusing on earthly riches and pleasures — here, the beautiful gardens and vineyards cultivated for luxury. It is a vivid image of idolatry: replacing trust in God with trust in one's own possessions and enjoyments. Such gardens were common in the ancient East and symbolized prosperity; the prophet uses it to criticize infidelity.
H5282.portee: This image speaks directly to us: we too, as Christians, risk allowing the pleasures of this world — comfort, beauty, prosperity — to divert us from God. The entry invites us to examine what we place our trust in. It reminds us that "ornamental plantings" are temporary, while a relationship with God alone is lasting and truly salvific.

sens: son of Benjamin and of the tribe of Israel
commander of the army of Syria afflicted with leprosy
H5283G.detail:
1. Naaman is first a name borne by a descendant of Benjamin listed among those who entered Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:21). He is a member of the patriarchal family that will later become a tribe of Israel.
2. Naaman is best known as the commander of the army of the king of Syria, afflicted with leprosy. Although powerful and respected, this serious illness rendered him unclean according to the Law. After following the instructions of the prophet Elisha — dipping seven times in the Jordan — he was completely healed and converted to the God of Israel.
H5283G.origine: The name Naaman means "pleasantness" or "agreeableness" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking grace and charm. It is a name borne in the tribe of Benjamin, but it became famous mainly due to the Syrian general whose story illustrates how human power and wealth cannot do anything against misfortune, and how humble obedience to the true God brings healing.
H5283G.emploi: Naaman appears in the Bible under two main identities. First as the son of Bela in the genealogy of Benjamin at the time of the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:21). But the most famous Naaman in the Bible is the Syrian commander of the king whose story occupies all of chapter 5 of the second book of Kings. Rich and powerful, he was nevertheless a slave to his disease. His account shows the contrast between worldly greatness and the unique power of God. His obedience to the words of Elisha, despite the apparent humiliation of the requested act (dipping in a small river), leads him to healing and true faith. It is a story of transformation: from proud denial to grateful acceptance.
H5283G.portee: The story of Naaman teaches that power and social status do not protect against misfortunes, and that only God can truly heal. It also shows how simple and humble obedience to God's words, even when it seems unprestigious, opens the way to transformation. For the Christian reader, Naaman embodies one who renounces his pride and finds salvation — an image of what it truly means to turn to God.

sens: Member of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela, living at the time of Egypt and the desert
Ancestor whose name gave that of the family of the Naamanites
H5283H.detail:
1. Naaman is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela. He is part of the family of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Numbers 26:40). His name appears in the genealogies of the people of Israel, testifying to his place in the ancient history of the chosen people.
2. From Naaman descends the family of the Naamanites, as indicated by the expression "of Naaman, the family of the Naamanites" (Numbers 26:40). Thus, the following generations perpetuated his memory by bearing the name of his descendants.
H5283H.origine: The name Naaman (נַעֲמָן) means "pleasantness" or "sweetness." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing what is pleasing or sweet. This name was borne by several important figures in biblical history, notably the famous commander of the Syrian army who was healed of leprosy by the prophet Elisha (although this Naaman is a different person). The diminutive Naamite (נַעֲמִי) designates the members of the family descending from this Benjaminite Naaman.
H5283H.emploi: Naaman appears twice in the provided biblical texts, both in a genealogical context. First in Numbers 26:40, at the time of the census of the Israelites in the desert, where he is listed among the sons of Bela with his brother Ard. Then in 1 Chronicles 8:4, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. These two mentions confirm his role as a patriarch founding a Benjaminite lineage, without any particular action reported about him. His importance is purely genealogical: he marks a branch of the descendants of Benjamin.

sens: Commander of the Syrian army during the divided monarchy
Mighty warrior afflicted with leprosy
Man who seeks healing from the prophet Elisha
Man converted to faith in the Lord
H5283I.detail:
1. Naaman is first the military chief of the king of Syria, a man of high rank and great influence, whom the king greatly esteems (2 Kings 5:1). His authority and prestige are immense: he commands the entire army.
2. Despite his strength and power, Naaman suffers from an incurable disease at the time: leprosy. This illness causes him great distress, he who is otherwise all-powerful in the military realm.
3. Driven by the hope of healing, Naaman goes to the prophet Elisha in Israel, accompanied by his entourage and precious gifts. He comes in person to the service of the king of Israel who has written to him (2 Kings 5:6, 5:9).
4. Naaman, after following the prophet's instructions and immersing himself in the Jordan, discovers true faith in the Lord. He renounces serving other gods and decides to offer sacrifices only to the Lord (2 Kings 5:17).
H5283I.origine: The name Naaman means "pleasant" or "sweet" in Hebrew — an ironic meaning since this powerful man will be humbled by illness. The account of Naaman is reported in 2 Kings 5, one of the great miracle and conversion narratives of the Old Testament. Naaman is not an Israelite but a Syrian: the sacred text shows that God's grace extends beyond the borders of Israel.
H5283I.emploi: Naaman appears 11 times in the text of 2 Kings 5, which recounts his entire story. He first embodies the powerful of the world, honored and feared, then the humiliated leper who must seek help outside his country. The text shows how his pride initially leads him to reject Elisha's instructions — he is indignant that the prophet does not come out to meet him and does something more spectacular to heal him (2 Kings 5:11). But gradually, Naaman learns humility, ultimately obeys the prophet, and becomes a believer in the Lord (2 Kings 5:17). His story illustrates the path of conversion: human pride must first be overcome by evil or impotence, and it is simple obedience to God that brings true healing.
H5283I.portee: The story of Naaman teaches the Christian reader that no barrier — neither nationality, distance, nor pride — can prevent God's grace from reaching those who seek it. It also shows that true power is not in wealth or military rank, but in obedience to God, even when it seems absurd to human reason. For the believer, it is a lesson in humility and trust: it is by accepting to lose what I pride myself on that I can be healed.

sens: Son of Bela, of the tribe of Benjamin, ancestor of Israel
H5283J.detail: Naaman is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. He is the son of Bela and is part of the family line that went down to Egypt with Jacob (1 Chronicles 8:7).
H5283J.origine: The name Naaman means "pleasant" or "sweet" in Hebrew, suggesting a positive connotation. It is a name borne by several biblical figures from different periods, marking the stability of this family name within the people of Israel.
H5283J.emploi: Naaman is mentioned exclusively in 1 Chronicles 8:7, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Bela, son of Benjamin. He is one of the distant ancestors of Israel whose name is reported to trace the lineage of God's chosen people.

sens: Inhabitant of Naamath, a city of which we know almost nothing
H5284.detail: 1. This term designates an inhabitant of a city called Naamath, apparently a little-known biblical locality. The book of Job applies this term to Zophar, one of Job's three friends who comes to visit him during his misfortune (Job 2:11). Although we do not know the exact location of this city, this demonym (name of the inhabitant) connects Zophar to a defined place of origin, as one would do for Eliphaz of Teman or Bildad of Shuh.
H5284.origine: The word comes from the city of Naamath, whose name means "pleasant" or "sweet." The demonym Naamite functions like all names of inhabitants: it is formed from the name of the place, much like one would say "a Parisian" for an inhabitant of Paris. The city of Naamath is mentioned only indirectly, through this term applied to Zophar; the Scriptures give us little detail about this locality.
H5284.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, solely in the book of Job, always to identify Zophar. In Job 2:11, it is first encountered when the three friends — Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar — learn of Job's misfortunes and decide to come to console him. Then Zophar of Naamath speaks twice (Job 11:1 and Job 20:1), and finally, he is mentioned one last time in Job 42:9 when the Lord asks the three friends to act according to His word. The term simply serves to identify who is speaking and where he comes from.
H5284.portee: This word reminds us that Job's friends came from diverse places and traditions, which makes their unity of heart in the desire to console him all the more remarkable. However, it will be discovered throughout the book that despite this initial solidarity, their explanations of Job's misfortune diverge deeply from the truth that God reveals.

sens: Dense and prickly plant, wild and untamed
Place of desolation or material poverty
Symbol of what is vain, miserable, or destined to disappear
Contrast with what is beautiful, cultivated, useful
H5285.detail:
1. A thornbush is a bushy and bristly plant, covered with spikes, that grows wild. In Isaiah 7:19, flies settle on the "bushes" of the desolate valleys: it is the image of misery and desert.
2. These bushes mark abandoned, barren, and unwelcoming places — the empty valleys and rocky crevices where fleeing insects seek refuge. They remind us of a ravaged land, devoid of ordered life or cultivation.
3. The thornbush symbolizes what is contemptible or worthless: in place of the thorn and the bramble, God will cause the cypress and the myrtle to grow (Isaiah 55:13). It is the transition from shame to glory, from the useless to the precious.
4. This contrast between the thorn and the noble trees — cypress, myrtle — shows that the thornbush embodies all that is inferior, wild, and destined to be transformed by the grace of God.
H5285.origine: The Hebrew word נַעֲצוּץ (na'atutsuts) evokes by its root the idea of prick and hardness — a sharp and hostile plant. It particularly describes the thorny bushes of the desert of the Levant, these low and bushy plants that yield neither edible fruit nor lasting shade. It is a typical plant of arid lands, a natural symbol of desolation.
H5285.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 7:19, it refers to the bushes of the desolate valleys where flies settle — an image of misfortune and plague. In Isaiah 55:13, the prophet announces that the thornbush will be replaced by the cypress and the bramble by the myrtle: it is the miraculous transformation of the curse into blessing. In both cases, the word paints the misery of the present that will yield to future restoration.
H5285.portee: This word reminds the believer that God does not allow the thorn to dominate forever. The thornbush symbolizes our arid lands, our seasons of sterility and desolation. Biblical hope consists of believing that God transforms the desert into a garden, shame into glory, the useless into a perpetual monument. It is a word of comfort for those going through trials.

sens: To make harsh and threatening cries, as carnivorous animals do
H5286.detail: 1. The word describes the deep and powerful cry made by large wild animals: the roars of lions and lion cubs. In Jeremiah 51:38, God announces that the enemies of Babylon "will roar together like lions" and "will growl like lion cubs" — an image of terror and unleashed brute force.
H5286.origine: The Hebrew word naʿar comes from a root that imitates the deep and rumbling sound of animal roaring. It is related to other Hebrew verbs expressing low and threatening cries. The starting image is that of the deep noise resonating from the throat of a wild beast.
H5286.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in Jeremiah 51:38, in a prophetic poem where God describes the ruin of Babylon: the enemy warriors will rush upon the city with as much ferocity and noise as hungry lions. The context is one of divine threat and imminent destruction.
H5286.portee: This word paints the image of brute force and immediate danger. It reminds us that God controls the violent powers of the world, even when they seem irresistible: the most terrifying roars are nothing compared to His justice.

sens: to make something fall or be removed by a sudden movement
to make disappear or move away
to free oneself from a constraint or grip
to be agitated or troubled
H5287.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to shake something to make it fall or empty. Moses shakes the sea by extending his hand, and it returned to its impetuosity (Exodus 14:27). Nehemiah shakes his cloak as a gesture of authority and rupture (Nehemiah 5:13), a symbolic act where this sudden movement represents a definitive separation.
2. By extension, to shake means to make disappear or remove far away: the wicked are shaken off the earth (Job 38:13), Pharaoh and his army are hurled into the sea (Psalms 136:15), meaning chased away and rejected.
3. The word also applies to the action of freeing oneself from a situation or grip. Samson wants to free himself from the Philistines who hold him (Judges 16:20), as if he were shaking off their chains.
4. Finally, to be shaken can describe the state of one who is agitated, troubled, or scattered: the psalmist says, "I am chased like a locust" (Psalms 109:23), an image of someone fleeing in disorder.
H5287.origine: The Hebrew verb נָעַר (na'ar) expresses the vigorous action of making tremble or wobble. Its root evokes the idea of sudden and unstable movement. The word is related to other Hebrew terms that describe agitation or trembling. In the Greek of the Septuagint, it is often rendered by σαλεύω (to shake) or ῥίπτω (to throw), which reinforce the idea of violent movement and rejection.
H5287.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Qal (simple form), Niphal (passive), and Piel (intensive). It is found in contexts of dramatic rupture: Exodus 14:27 and Psalms 136:15 report how God shakes and drowns Pharaoh and his troops in the sea. In Judges 16:20, Samson wants to free himself from the grip of his enemies. Nehemiah 5:13 uses the gesture of shaking his cloak as a symbol of a solemn separation, accompanied by a curse. In Job 38:13, God speaks of shaking the wicked off the earth. The word is therefore mainly used for ruptures, rejections, or liberations marked by force and authority.
H5287.portee: This verb invites us to meditate on the power of God, who shakes the wicked kingdoms and frees His people. It also shows that prayer and righteous management sometimes require radical ruptures, without hesitation: Nehemiah shakes his cloak as a prophetic gesture of separation from evil. For the believer, to shake also means to free oneself from what hinders, to accept that God may shake our certainties to establish us in the truth.

sens: Boy or adolescent, son in early or middle age
Young adult or of marriageable age
Servant, personal aide, assistant to a man or leader
Young person in general, opposed to the old
H5288.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a young boy, from a small child to an adolescent. When Hagar sees Ishmael dying of thirst in the desert, the Bible says "the child" cried (Genesis 21:17): it is the same word. Samson, in his mother's womb, is called "young" because he is not yet born (Judges 13:5).
2. It can also refer to a young man of strength and responsibility, of age to fight or lead. When Judah tells Joseph that a "young man" (Benjamin) cannot leave Canaan (Genesis 44:22), he is speaking of a valuable adolescent.
3. The most common meaning in the Bible is that of servant or personal assistant. In Genesis 14:24, Abraham speaks of the "young" men who walked with him into battle: they are his servants. In 1 Kings 20:17, the "servants" of the leaders go out with their weapons — the same Hebrew word. It was a relative title of honor: a servant of the king was a man of power.
4. Finally, the word can simply contrast youth with old age, as in Esther 3:13 where the edict targets the Jews "young and old": here, people are classified by age.
H5288.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of shaking, stirring, being active and vigorous. A "young" person is primarily one who has the vigor of youth. Various forms of the word appear in proper names and other biblical contexts. The notion of "servant" comes from the fact that strong young people naturally served mature men and leaders: youth and personal service went together in ancient Near Eastern culture.
H5288.emploi: The word appears 221 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis and the historical books. It primarily means "boy" or "child" — Samuel as a child in the sanctuary is a "young" (1 Samuel 2:18), Ishmael as a young is a "child" (Genesis 21:17). But very often, it means "servant" or "assistant": Abraham has young men in battle (Genesis 14:24), Samson has a young man guiding him (Judges 16:26). Between these two poles, the word also covers young men in general, of age to act — fight, marry, work. The context leans towards one or the other meaning: the age of the character, his role, and the domain (family, war, service) indicate whether one is speaking of a child, a young adult, or a servant.
H5288.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Bible values youth not as rebellion or inexperience, but as a strength in service. A young person can serve God with vigor and responsibility: Samuel as a child heard the call of the Lord (1 Samuel 3:8). Youth is no less worthy than age; it has its place and dignity in God's plan. This also invites one to see the servants of the Bible not as humiliated slaves, but as men of trust and relative power in a society organized by ranks.

sens: woolly herd animal, small livestock
weak and vulnerable animal that needs to be guided and cared for
people or community in a relationship of dependence on God or a leader
H5289.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete animal: a sheep, this small woolly ruminant that moves in a herd. In Zechariah 11:16, the bad shepherd refuses to seek "the younger" of the sheep — he even refuses to care for the most vulnerable.

2. The sheep also evokes the biblical image of weakness and dependence. It cannot survive alone: it needs a shepherd to guide it, care for it when it is wounded, and find it pasture. In Zechariah 11:16, it is by contrast: the bad shepherd does not heal the wounded, he does not care for the healthy — he abandons his sheep.

3. The Bible uses "sheep" to speak of the people of God or the community of believers. Just as sheep need a human shepherd, the people need a just and caring guide. An unworthy shepherd (as in Zechariah 11) diverts this responsibility.
H5289.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of lightness, fragility. The sheep is a light animal, easily frightened, that disperses quickly. This is why the image of the shepherd who gathers and protects the flock is so powerful in the Bible: it symbolizes the relationship between God and His people, or between a leader and those entrusted to him.
H5289.emploi: This word appears only once in this specific usage in Zechariah 11:16. The passage paints a negative portrait: a false shepherd who should care for the sheep (feed them, heal them, seek the lost) but who, on the contrary, exploits and abandons them. It is a critique of the poor management of God's people by leaders who forget their responsibility.
H5289.portee: This vision of the bad shepherd and his neglected sheep challenges the reader regarding the quality of spiritual leadership. It shows that those charged with guiding God's people have a sacred responsibility: to care for the weak, seek the lost, heal the wounded. For the believer, it is a call to recognize what it means to be entrusted to a true shepherd, or to exercise care for others with faithfulness and tenderness.

sens: The period of life extending from childhood to adulthood
The state or condition of the young man, his inexperience and fragility
The physical vigor and energy characteristic of this age
Life considered in its beginnings and development
H5290.detail:
1. Youth is primarily the period of life between childhood and adulthood, a time of growth and formation. It is the age of beginnings: one who returns to the "days of his youth" (Job 33:25) becomes vigorous again as he was at the beginning of his life.

2. It also designates the condition of the young, characterized by a certain fragility and exposure to dangers. The Bible notes that some "perish in their youth" (Job 36:14), due to a lack of wisdom and protection.

3. The word evokes the strength and physical vigor of this age: the flesh regains "more freshness" when one returns to youth, that is, to health and vitality.

4. By extension, youth also encompasses the entire early years, the personal history in its origins: being "laden with terrors from youth" (Psalms 88:16) means having suffered since the beginnings of life.
H5290.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of stirring, moving, agitating — a natural image for childhood and youth, ages of movement and energy. In the same family, other terms related to active life and change can be found. The word expresses less the innocence of childhood (which other terms denote) than the dynamic, mobile period of youth.
H5290.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, mainly in the books of wisdom and lamentations. In Job (33:25 and 36:14), it first describes the renewal of physical vigor, then the vulnerability of young people to waywardness. Psalm 88:16 uses it to evoke a life marked by suffering from its beginnings. Finally, Proverbs 29:21 shows how the "pampered" childhood prepares for bad character. Each usage emphasizes the contrast between the carefreeness or natural fragility of this age and the realities (renewal, danger, suffering, education) that life confronts it with.
H5290.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that youth is a crucial time: a moment of vigor, certainly, but also of vulnerability and formation. It requires vigilance, wisdom, and support — which only God can provide durably. Recognizing the young in their strengths and fragilities means training them with tenderness and firmness.

sens: Girl or young woman of marriageable age
Servant or housemaid
Young woman in a marital or conjugal relationship
H5291.detail:
1. The most common meaning: a girl or a young woman, generally of marriageable age. It is the image of a young, healthy person capable of bearing children. In Genesis 24:14, Abraham's servant seeks the young woman who will become Isaac's wife; in Deuteronomy 22:15, the signs of virginity of a young woman are discussed to prove her innocence.
2. A servant or a woman employed in the service of a household. She is not free, but she may hold a position of trust. Ruth 2:5-6 mentions this: Boaz asks who this young woman is among the harvesters; she is Naomi's servant, poor but industrious.
3. A woman united to a man by marriage or in a similar relationship. In 1 Samuel 25:42, Abigail becomes David's wife by leaving with him, accompanied by her young women. The word can also refer to a concubine or, in sad cases, a woman who is a victim of abuse (Deuteronomy 22:23-29, where the law protects the engaged or unmarried young woman).
H5291.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes youth and strength. It is related to the word for "boy" (nar) and specifically denotes the feminine version. The root emphasizes the idea of youth and vitality — what is young, what begins, what has energy. It is a purely Hebrew word, with no direct Greek equivalent in the Septuagint.
H5291.emploi: The word appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Judges, Ruth, and Esther. It often designates young women in the context of marriage or domestic life: Rebekah in Genesis 24, the four hundred young virgin girls in Judges 21:12, Esther at the king's court. It also appears in laws regarding the protection of women (Deuteronomy 22), where the text distinguishes between the engaged young woman, the virgin young woman, and the one who has suffered harm. The word can carry a shade of vulnerability (a young woman without protection) or strength (a faithful servant like Ruth). In Proverbs 31:15, a virtuous woman "gives her servants their tasks."
H5291.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, young women are not merely silent figures: they are actors in the story of salvation. Rebekah chooses to go with Abraham's servant; Esther becomes queen; Ruth becomes the ancestor of King David. The word also emphasizes how the laws of the Torah specifically protect young women from exploitation. For today's Christian, this invites us to honor young women, to listen to them, and to protect them — as God Himself requires.

sens: Location on the southern border of the territory of Ephraim
H5292A.detail: 1. Naaratha is a place that marked the southern limit of the territory assigned to the tribe of Ephraim during the division of Canaan. Its name means "young woman" in Hebrew, but it refers here to a city or geographical landmark. In Joshua 16:7, it is mentioned among the locations that trace the eastern border of Ephraim: from Janoach, the boundary descended to Atharoth and Naaratha, then touched Jericho before joining the Jordan. This locality thus belonged to the strip of territory located between the mountain of Ephraim and the valley of the Jordan, in the region of Jericho.
H5292A.origine: The name Naaratha comes from the Hebrew נַעֲרָה (na'arah), which literally means "young woman" or "virgin." It is possible that this place received this poetic name or that "young woman" became a geographical designation — a practice known in ancient territories. The Hebrew name is also known in the variant Naaran (נַעֲרָן), which likely designates the same place or a locality very close to the same area.
H5292A.emploi: Naaratha appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 16:7, where it is included in the description of the borders of the territory of Ephraim. It is cited alongside other localities like Janoach, Atharoth, and Jericho, to precisely delineate the eastern perimeter of this tribe. This purely geographical and administrative role shows that it was a well-known and identifiable landmark at the time of the writing of the Book of Joshua.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H5292B.detail: Naara is a woman of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogies of the book of Chronicles. She is the second wife of Ashhur and the mother of four sons: Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari (1 Chronicles 4:5-6). Her name means "young woman" in ancient Hebrew, perhaps recalling her status as a young woman at the time of her marriage.
H5292B.origine: The name Naara derives from a Hebrew root meaning "young woman" or "young girl." It is a descriptive name that evokes youth or adolescence, although no data really specifies this woman's age at the time of her marriage to Ashhur.
H5292B.emploi: Naara appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 4:5-6, in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. These verses identify her as Ashhur's wife and list her four sons. She is one of the many female figures in biblical genealogies, often mentioned simply as wives and mothers to establish lineages.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David
H5293.detail: Naaraï is a man who lived during the divided monarchy of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:37, as one of David's "mighty men" (or powerful warriors). He was the son of Ezbai and from Arbah. His name means "servant" or "young woman," which may seem surprising for a soldier, but Hebrew names were not always directly related to the role or character of the person who bore them.
H5293.origine: The name Naaraï (נַעֲרַי) comes from a Hebrew root meaning "young woman" or "servant." It is an uncommon name in the Bible. It appears only in the list of David's warriors preserved in 1 Chronicles 11, which enumerates the exceptional men who supported the king during his life.
H5293.emploi: Naaraï is cited only once in the entire Bible: in 1 Chronicles 11:37. He appears in a list of renowned warriors in the service of King David, alongside names like Hetsro of Carmel. This list celebrates the valiant men who contributed to establishing David's kingdom. The context shows that Naaraï was an elite soldier, a man whose courage and loyalty to David distinguished him among the other warriors of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
Son of Schemaiah and father of Eljoenaï
Descendant of King David in the royal line
Member of the royal family after the exile
H5294G.detail:
1. Néaria is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the divided monarchy, after the return from exile. His name literally means "servant of the Lord."
2. He is the son of Schemaiah and the father of three children: Eljoenaï, Hezekiah, and Azrikam (1 Chronicles 3:23). He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of King David.
3. Néaria is one of the six sons of Schemaiah, alongside Hattush, Jigeal, Bariah, and Shaphat (1 Chronicles 3:22). This lineage shows the continuity of David's royal family after the Babylonian exile.
H5294G.origine: The name Néaria is composed of two Hebrew elements: "na'ar" (young man, servant) and "Yah" (abbreviated form of the Lord). It thus means "servant of the Lord" or "young man of the Lord." This type of theophoric name (containing the divine name) was common among Jews to express their dependence on God.
H5294G.emploi: Néaria appears twice in the Holy Scriptures, both in the first book of Chronicles, which traces the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:22 as one of the sons of Schemaiah, and in 1 Chronicles 3:23 in the genealogy of his own sons. These mentions are part of a genealogical list of the royal house of David, which aimed to establish the legitimate continuity of Davidic royalty after the return from exile in Babylon.

sens: Military leader of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of King Hezekiah
H5294H.detail: Nearia is a warrior from the tribe of Simeon who, under the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, commanded five hundred men. Along with his brothers Pelathia, Rephaja, and Uziel, he led his troops to the mountain of Seir to drive the Amalekites out of that region. This is the only passage in the Bible where he is mentioned.
H5294H.origine: The name Nearia means "servant of the Lord" or "one who serves the Lord." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ner" (servant) and the name of God. This type of name was common in Israel to express dependence on God and to mark a religious consecration from birth.
H5294H.emploi: Nearia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:42, where he is presented as one of the four sons of Jischeï (or Ishi) in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon. At that time, during the reign of Hezekiah, he held a military position as a leader or captain. His role was to lead soldiers into battle against the Amalekites, a traditional enemy of Israel. This simple account illustrates how men of faith and courage acted during the religious revival of Hezekiah's reign.
H5294H.portee: Nearia reminds us that God used faithful warriors to defend His people and reclaim territories. His name, which means "servant of the Lord," invites the reader to see these military exploits not as acts of personal glory, but as service rendered to God and His plan for Israel.

sens: City on the eastern border of the territory of Ephraim
H5295.detail: Naaran is a city that marks the eastern boundary of the lands possessed by the tribe of Ephraim. It is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 7:28, where it is listed among the cities that the sons of Ephraim owned and inhabited, alongside Bethel, Gezer, and Shechem. It thus represents an important geographical landmark of the Ephraimite territory in the post-exilic period.
H5295.origine: The name Naaran literally means "youthful" or "one who rejects shoots." It can be associated with the concept of youth or vigor. The alternative form Naarah (נַעֲרָה) also refers to this same city and comes from a root related to youth or greenness.
H5295.emploi: Naaran appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:28. This passage lists the cities of the territory of Ephraim during the period of return from exile or the reign of Solomon. Naaran is explicitly placed to the east of the territory, while other cities like Gezer and Shechem mark the western boundaries. Its status as a border city makes it significant for precisely delineating the territorial possessions of the tribe.

sens: Coarse textile fiber obtained by beating flax
Dry and flammable material, easily consumed by fire
H5296.detail:
1. The term 'étoupe' refers to the coarse and short fiber obtained when preparing flax by beating it to clean it: it is the waste from flax processing, but it can be used to make ropes or ties. Samson breaks cords of étoupe as easily as burned thread (Judges 16:9), which illustrates the extreme fragility of this material in the face of heat.
2. Étoupe symbolizes what burns easily and without resistance, a dry, flammable, and insubstantial material. The prophet Isaiah uses it to describe the helplessness of the sinner: the strong man, in his pride, becomes as fragile as étoupe, and his work burns like a mere spark (Isaiah 1:31).
H5296.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of shaking or beating, as it is by beating the flax fibers that this étoupe is obtained. It is a humble and low-value material in ancient daily life, but it becomes in Scripture a poignant image of fragility and divine judgment.
H5296.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in the two provided passages. In Judges 16:9, it describes cords that Samson breaks effortlessly, demonstrating his superhuman strength: étoupe here is a concrete term drawn from textile work. In Isaiah 1:31, the same word becomes an image of judgment: before God, the proud man and his carnal work are as insubstantial as étoupe in the face of fire; they will burn and disappear. Both uses play on the contrast: what binds Samson breaks effortlessly, and what pretends to endure without God is annihilated in judgment.
H5296.portee: This word reminds the believer of the fragility of all that strays from God and His justice. Like étoupe consumed by fire, the plans and works of the carnal man have no eternal solidity. It is an invitation to build on the rock of the Lord rather than on the sand of rebellion, and to recognize that our strength, like Samson's, comes only from God alone.

sens: Capital of ancient Egypt
Seat of Egyptian political and religious power
Symbol of Egyptian might
H5297.detail:
1. Noph is the Hebrew name for Memphis, the great capital of Egypt located in Lower Egypt. It was the political, administrative, and religious center of the country for centuries. The Bible mentions it as an important and prestigious city (Isaiah 19:13 speaks of the "princes of Noph").
2. Noph represents the power and authority of Egypt. God announces judgments against this city: it will become a desert (Jeremiah 46:19), its idols will be destroyed, and there will no longer be a prince of the land (Ezekiel 30:13).
3. For the Jews in exile, Noph is both a refuge and a place of danger. The Bible mentions Jewish colonies in Noph, Tahpanhes, and Migdol (Jeremiah 44:1), and these cities are warned to prepare for captivity when the sword comes (Jeremiah 46:14).
H5297.origine: Noph comes from the Egyptian name of the city (nfr in ancient Egyptian, meaning "beautiful"), which the Hebrews adapted to their language. An alternative, Moph (מֹף), also exists in biblical texts. This name specifically designates the ancient city, center of worship for the god Ptah.
H5297.emploi: Noph appears 7 times in the Bible, exclusively in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) in the 7th-6th centuries B.C. It is always mentioned in the context of divine judgment against Egypt. The princes of Noph are depicted as foolish and leading the people astray (Isaiah 19:13). Jeremiah announces imminent destruction: the sword devours around the city (Jeremiah 46:14), and it becomes a desert without inhabitants (Jeremiah 46:19). Ezekiel proclaims the annihilation of its idols and the collapse of princely power (Ezekiel 30:13).
H5297.portee: Noph reminds us that even the greatest human powers, fortified by wealth and idols, are subject to God's judgment. Its decline, announced by the prophets, affirms that the glory of empires is fleeting and that only God remains eternal. For believers, it is a call not to place their trust in earthly powers.

sens: Son of Jitschar, of the tribe of Levi, at the time of the Exodus
One of the sons of King David born in Jerusalem
H5298G.detail:
1. Népheg is a man from the tribe of Levi, son of Jitschar and grandson of Kehath. He lived at the time of the Exodus and appears in the genealogy of the Levites (Exodus 6:21). He was the brother of Korah, Zicri, and Shélomith.
2. A second character of the same name is mentioned in the royal genealogies: one of the sons of King David, born in Jerusalem during David's reign.
H5298G.origine: The Hebrew name "Népheg" means "bud" or "shoot," an image of growth and new life. It is a name that evokes fertility and multiplication, an important characteristic for the families of the people of Israel.
H5298G.emploi: The name Népheg designates two distinct characters in the Old Testament. The first is a Levite from the time of the Exodus, mentioned only once in Exodus 6:21 in the genealogy of the tribe of Levi, serving to identify the descendants of Kehath. The second is a son of King David, cited in the royal genealogies of Jerusalem.

sens: Son of David born in Jerusalem
One of the sons of Izhar, grandson of Kohath, of the tribe of Levi
H5298H.detail: 1. Népheg is one of the sons of King David, born to him in Jerusalem during his reign. He appears in the list of his children in Jerusalem, alongside his brothers Noga, Japhia, and Elishama (2 Samuel 5:15; 1 Chronicles 3:7; 1 Chronicles 14:6). Although he is a son of the king, the Bible reports nothing particular about his life or deeds: he is mentioned only as a member of the royal family.
H5298H.origine: The name Népheg literally means "young shoot" or "bud," evoking the image of a plant emerging from the ground. This name belongs to a family of Hebrew words denoting growth and youth. It appears that several men bore this name in the history of Israel, notably a Levite during the time of the Exodus.
H5298H.emploi: Népheg is mentioned three times in the Bible, solely in the genealogical lists of the sons of King David. He appears in two parallel accounts: 2 Samuel 5:15 lists the sons born to David in Jerusalem after his reign was established, and 1 Chronicles 3:7 and 1 Chronicles 14:6 repeat this same genealogy. These three references are the only mentions of this Népheg son of David in the Bible. He plays no particular role in history; he is simply recorded in the royal succession.

sens: Kitchen or agricultural utensil used to separate fine elements from coarse elements
Figuratively, that which separates, judges, or sorts by distinguishing the good from the bad
H5299A.detail:
1. A crible is a practical tool used in the kitchen or on the farm: it is a kind of sieve made with mesh or holes that allow grains, flour, or other powdered materials to pass through while rejecting debris and impurities. It is shaken so that small particles fall through while larger pieces remain on top. In Isaiah 30:28, God uses the image of the crible to describe how He will sift the nations with destruction: just as a tool separates grain from waste, God distinguishes and separates peoples.
2. Figuratively, a crible becomes an image of that which judges, sorts, or tests people: it separates the sincere from the hypocrites, the faithful from the unfaithful, just as fire separates pure gold from impure metal.
H5299A.origine: The Hebrew word nâphâh comes from a root that evokes the idea of shaking or winnowing. The crible is literally the instrument that accomplishes this action: the sieve is shaken so that light materials escape while what matters remains. This image has naturally transitioned to a figurative sense, speaking of that which sorts, tests, or judges.
H5299A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 30:28, where it poetically describes divine judgment. In this passage, the prophet announces that the breath of the Lord, like a mighty torrent, will sift the nations, meaning they will be judged and separated. This judgment is understood as a process of discernment: the nations will be sifted through destruction. The image of the crible reinforces the idea of an inevitable and decisive separation.
H5299A.portee: This image of the crible reminds the reader that God judges, sorts, and discerns. It invites one to take the prophetic warning seriously: no one can hide from God; His judgment sifts even the nations. For the believer, this also speaks of testing and purification: God tests faith to extract what is true and lasting. It is an image that is both terrible and purifying.

sens: Elevated place, summit or high point of terrain
Mountainous region or mountain range
H5299B.detail:
1. The word designates a place that rises above the surrounding terrain, a dominant point. In Joshua 11:2, the "heights of Dor" refer to the mountainous region that overlooks this coastal locality, where the Canaanite kings gathered to confront Joshua.
2. More broadly, the term evokes a geographical area characterized by its rugged relief and elevations. It is a region naturally fortified by its hills and slopes, difficult to access and easy to defend — which explains why the kings gathered there for battle.
H5299B.origine: The Hebrew word napha comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising, dominating in height. It describes a geographical space characterized by its altitude and marked relief. It is the natural term to designate the mountainous areas of Israel and Canaan, which armies had to cross and whose strategic passages needed to be controlled.
H5299B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 11:2. It is used to geographically locate the gathering of the northern kings against Joshua: precisely in the "heights of Dor," this coastal region fortified by its hills. The military context shows that "height" does not simply refer to an abstract elevation, but to a real strategic terrain where armies positioned themselves.
H5299B.portee: This passage reminds us that geographical obstacles — mountains, valleys, heights — do not prevent the victory that God grants. The kings gathered in the most inaccessible places, but Joshua, led by the Lord, defeated them there. This invites the reader to trust in God rather than in material defenses.

sens: To keep in memory, to retain
To maintain intact in one's heart or mind
H5202.detail:
1. To keep in memory, to retain: the word denotes the action of preserving something precious by keeping it present in the mind. In Daniel 7:28, Daniel "conserves" the mysterious words of his vision in his heart — he does not forget them, he carries them with him like a treasure that one does not let go of.
2. To maintain intact in one's heart or mind: it is also the inner vigilance that protects what one holds as important, keeping it away from forgetfulness or neglect. This is why this Hebrew and Aramaic verb is naturally used for one who keeps the words of God or the events that have marked them.
H5202.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from the same Hebrew root as נָטַר (na.tar, H5201, "to keep," "to conserve"). The root evokes the idea of watching over something, holding it firmly. In Hebrew and Aramaic, this family of words applies to one who keeps a secret, who watches over a burden, or who preserves a memory in their heart. It is a word that emphasizes the personal responsibility of one who retains something precious.
H5202.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament (Daniel 7:28). It is a moment where the prophet Daniel, after receiving a troubling and enigmatic vision about the future of kingdoms, carefully keeps these mysterious words in his heart. The context shows someone who, shaken by what he has heard, does not let these revelations slip away: he conserves them, reflects on them, carries them within him like a sacred burden from which he must not turn away.
H5202.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reminds us that receiving the word of God is not passive: we must keep it, return to it, and allow it to work within us. Just as Daniel keeps the words of his vision despite the turmoil and fear, the believer is called to conserve God's promises and revelations in their heart, away from forgetfulness and distractions, so that they may gradually transform them.
